name: Exploratory Analysis Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in exploratory analysis work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.
content:
This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in exploratory analysis work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Surface known limitations of a chosen exploratory analysis approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
2. Validate exploratory analysis outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
3. Re-check edge cases relevant to exploratory analysis (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
4. When multiple exploratory analysis strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
5. Keep exploratory analysis outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
6. Document any non-obvious exploratory analysis decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
7. Keep exploratory analysis changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
8. When exploratory analysis guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
9. State assumptions about exploratory analysis explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated exploratory analysis concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not silently drop exploratory analysis edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not skip documenting exploratory analysis assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid introducing new exploratory analysis abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for exploratory analysis, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
